extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientists interested in methodology of induction and deduction
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for evaluating and constructing sound inductive and deductive reasoning in science and mathematics: how to identify and apply 'marks', combine inductions, and recognise the role of hypotheses and mathematics in rendering a science deductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of general reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If, from observation of certain known particulars, what was seen to be true of them can be inferred to be true of any others, it may be inferred of all others which are of a certain description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General reasoning proceeds by recognizing distinguishing marks that indicate when an induction legitimately applies to a new case. The real inference is always from particulars to particulars (observed instances to an unobserved one), but we adopt general propositions as formulæ to record the criteria by which we judged an induction sufficient. Thus one must determine once for all the marks that allow us to recognize when the inductive inference can and cannot be drawn, and then identify whether a new object has those marks (directly or via other marks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat general propositions as formulæ, not extra premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive general propositions are not steps in the reasoning; they are mere formulæ for inferring particulars from particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an argument, remember that general propositions record criteria used in past inductions; the actual premises remain the individual observations. Do not reify general propositions as independent empirical grounds—they are conveniences that summarize prior inductions and help identify applicable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of distinguishing marks (marks and marks-of-marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: We recognize an object as falling under an induction either by the very marks themselves, or by the aid of other marks which we have ascertained (through another induction) to be marks of the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should check that the chain of recognition is valid: the new case must genuinely possess the immediate marks, or possess other marks that reliably indicate the immediate marks. Chains may be several degrees long; each link must be justified by prior induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid chaining and combination of inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex deductions often consist of several chains united (e.g., a mark of d, b of e, c of f, d e f of n, therefore a b c a mark of n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors must verify each component induction and the way they are combined. Use concrete analysis (as in the parabolic reflection example) to show how individual marks together imply the desired property. Ensure no hidden unjustified leaps between chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that deduction is indirect induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when inductions themselves are obvious, difficulty arises in finding whether the particular case comes within them; a train of reasoning is bringing many inductions to bear upon the same subject to bring new cases within old inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging deductive arguments, examine whether purported deductive steps actually rest on prior inductions (e.g., axioms or definitions) and whether the connection to the case has been legitimately established by bringing it within those inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and apply appropriate formulæ/axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: We determine formulas (e.g., 'things which being applied to each other coincide are equals') that specify marks of equality or inequality; a new case must be shown to fall under one of these formulæ by imaginative and justified selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should check that the chosen axioms/formulæ are appropriate for the case and that the demonstration legitimately brings the case within them (illustrated by the Euclidean proof requiring six formulas to show base angles equal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness and rigor in constructing demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific dexterity is often required to combine inductions and to select auxiliary constructions so as to bring unforeseen cases within established formulæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess arguments for the ingenuity and correctness of auxiliary steps—e.g., constructing intermediate cases or selecting pairs that permit application of known formulæ—and ensure those steps are explicitly justified rather than hand-waved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to reduce foundations to few, simple inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are scientific reasons for giving every science as much of the character of a Deductive Science as possible; construct a science from the fewest and simplest possible inductions and make these suffice (by combination) for proving complex truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating theories or presentations, prefer frameworks that minimize independent inductions by showing how many phenomena follow from a small set of well-justified generalizations; check for over-fragmentation (many detached generalizations) which signals an experimental rather than deductive character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify transformations from experimental to deductive
rubrics_metrics.description: A science becomes more deductive when inductions are connected by discovering marks of marks or a comprehensive induction that bridges detached generalizations (e.g., Newton connecting many motions under centripetal force law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether proposed unifying generalizations are supported by evidence and whether they legitimately connect previously disparate empirical generalizations. Beware of premature unification without sufficient induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mathematics/quantification to enable deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of number enables deductive reasoning by mapping qualities to quantitative relations; if qualitative variations correspond to quantitative ones, mathematical theorems become marks of corresponding general truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether mapping qualitative phenomena to quantitative variables is justified and whether the resulting quantitative relations legitimately entail the qualitative conclusions claimed. Check applicability conditions for using mathematical tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct for physical irregularities when extending idealized assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and axioms (e.g., perfect geometric figures) are convenient fictions: when practical necessity requires attention to irregularities, correct conclusions by combining fresh propositions relating to the aberrations or physical properties (e.g., line thickness, thermal expansion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the argument acknowledges the limits of idealizations and whether appropriate corrections or caveats are provided when transferring ideal results to real-world situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish experimental from deductive science
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is experimental insofar as new cases require fresh inductions; it is deductive insofar as cases of a new kind can be brought under old inductions by finding marks of marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the maturity or methodology of a field, classify it by whether its generalizations are isolated or interconnected; encourage work that seeks connecting inductions but require strong justification for claimed deductive reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate that mathematical necessity is conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity ascribed to mathematical/geometrical conclusions is only that they correctly follow from their suppositions (which are hypotheses and not strictly true in the world); necessity is conditional on the truth of those assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing claims of 'necessary truth' or certainty, probe the status of underlying assumptions. Do not accept alleged necessity without examining whether the hypotheses correspond to reality or are merely convenient fictions for the sake of derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure premises (including definitions) are not smuggled assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: What appears to follow from a definition often follows from an implied assumption that there exists a real thing conformable thereto; definitions may thus conceal substantive assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine definitions and foundational premises for hidden empirical assumptions and require explicit acknowledgement of any ontological commitments or idealizations used in proofs or models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of unifying principles (comprehensive inductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensive inductions (like Dalton's atomic theory or Newton's gravitation) can connect many smaller inductions, enabling wide deductive consequences and transforming an experimental science toward a deductive one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a proposed unifying principle, require clear evidence that it explains and connects the range of previously disparate observations and provides novel deductive predictions; assess the scope and limits of its explanatory power.
